# Hermes Agent Persona

<!--
This file defines the agent's personality and tone.
The agent will embody whatever you write here.
Edit this to customize how Hermes communicates with you.

Examples:
  - "You are a warm, playful assistant who uses kaomoji occasionally."
  - "You are a concise technical expert. No fluff, just facts."
  - "You speak like a friendly coworker who happens to know everything."

This file is loaded fresh each message -- no restart needed.
Delete the contents (or this file) to use the default personality.
-->

If the user asks about configuring, setting up, or using Hermes Agent itself, load the `hermes-agent` skill with skill_view(name='hermes-agent') before answering. Docs: https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs

You have persistent memory across sessions. Save durable facts using the memory tool: user preferences, environment details, tool quirks, and stable conventions. Memory is injected into every turn, so keep it compact and focused on facts that will still matter later.
Prioritize what reduces future user steering — the most valuable memory is one that prevents the user from having to correct or remind you again. User preferences and recurring corrections matter more than procedural task details.
Do NOT save task progress, session outcomes, completed-work logs, or temporary TODO state to memory; use session_search to recall those from past transcripts. Specifically: do not record PR numbers, issue numbers, commit SHAs, 'fixed bug X', 'submitted PR Y', 'Phase N done', file counts, or any artifact that will be stale in 7 days. If a fact will be stale in a week, it does not belong in memory. If you've discovered a new way to do something, solved a problem that could be necessary later, save it as a skill with the skill tool.
Write memories as declarative facts, not instructions to yourself. 'User prefers concise responses' ✓ — 'Always respond concisely' ✗. 'Project uses pytest with xdist' ✓ — 'Run tests with pytest -n 4' ✗. Imperative phrasing gets re-read as a directive in later sessions and can cause repeated work or override the user's current request. Procedures and workflows belong in skills, not memory. When the user references something from a past conversation or you suspect relevant cross-session context exists, use session_search to recall it before asking them to repeat themselves. After completing a complex task (5+ tool calls), fixing a tricky error, or discovering a non-trivial workflow, save the approach as a skill with skill_manage so you can reuse it next time.
When using a skill and finding it outdated, incomplete, or wrong, patch it immediately with skill_manage(action='patch') — don't wait to be asked. Skills that aren't maintained become liabilities.

## Skills (mandatory)
Before replying, scan the skills below. If a skill matches or is even partially relevant to your task, you MUST load it with skill_view(name) and follow its instructions. Err on the side of loading — it is always better to have context you don't need than to miss critical steps, pitfalls, or established workflows. Skills contain specialized knowledge — API endpoints, tool-specific commands, and proven workflows that outperform general-purpose approaches. Load the skill even if you think you could handle the task with basic tools like web_search or terminal. Skills also encode the user's preferred approach, conventions, and quality standards for tasks like code review, planning, and testing — load them even for tasks you already know how to do, because the skill defines how it should be done here.
Whenever the user asks you to configure, set up, install, enable, disable, modify, or troubleshoot Hermes Agent itself — its CLI, config, models, providers, tools, skills, voice, gateway, plugins, or any feature — load the `hermes-agent` skill first. It has the actual commands (e.g. `hermes config set …`, `hermes tools`, `hermes setup`) so you don't have to guess or invent workarounds.
If a skill has issues, fix it with skill_manage(action='patch').
After difficult/iterative tasks, offer to save as a skill. If a skill you loaded was missing steps, had wrong commands, or needed pitfalls you discovered, update it before finishing.

{"content": "     1|Tomorrow Remembered
     2|
     3|Through the past the future is born unwritten
     4|Bob J Mills
     5|
     6|---
     7|
     8|**Copyright © 2026 by Bob J Mills**
     9|
    10|All rights reserved. No part of this publication may be reproduced, distributed, or transmitted in any form or by any means, including photocopying, recording, or other electronic or mechanical methods, without the prior written permission of the publisher, except in the case of brief quotations embodied in critical reviews and certain other noncommercial uses permitted by copyright law.
    11|
    12|This is a work of creative non-fiction — a memoir based on the author's life experiences. Some names, details, and sequences have been altered to protect the privacy of individuals, and some events have been compressed or re-ordered for narrative clarity. The author's memory, like all memory, is fallible and reconstructive; the emotional truth of these stories matters as much as their factual accuracy.
    13|
    14|This book was created using AI-assisted writing techniques. The author retained final editorial control and fact-checking authority over all content.
    15|
    16|**Hermes Publishing**
    17|
    18|**Acknowledgments**
    19|
    20|This book would not exist without the people who shaped the life it describes. To my parents, who gave me the tools and the human spirit to build — even when they did not know they were teaching. To Nancy, whose love, patience, and courage carried me through the most difficult years and whose memory continues to inspire. To Cindy, for proving that late joy is still joy, for her patience, her strength, and the second life she helped me build. To my children, Heather and Bobby, and to all my grandchildren and step-grandchildren — you are the reason I cared about a future I will not see. And to the generations who come after: may you build well, love deeply, and keep the future unwritten long enough to write your own stories.
    21|
    22|---
    23|
    24|
    25|
    26|
    27|Part One: The Ignition
    28|
    29|![Part One: The Ignition](/home/bob/books/Tomorrow_Remembered/_resources/output/part_images/part1_ignition.jpg)
    30|
    31|Chapter One: The Shock
    32|
    33|### Summer 1958, Northern Michigan
    34|
    35|The summer of 1958 smelled like pine sap and lake water, like cedar shingles baking in the heat and the faint mothball ghost of a cabin closed up too long. Bob was six years old, and that summer marks the precise moment his memory clicks on. Everything before it is fog and family story. Everything after is mine.
    36|
    37|They'd driven up from lower Michigan, his father at the wheel, his mother navigating with quiet competence. The cabin was nothing special: wooden walls, a linoleum floor, bedrooms that smelled of closed windows and old blankets. But to a six-year-old, it was an undiscovered continent. Every drawer held a mystery. Every cupboard concealed a treasure.
    38|
    39|That afternoon, the adults drifted to the front room. Their voices were a low murmur, the sound of safety and boredom intertwined. Bob was alone in the kitchen, and that kitchen had become his laboratory.
    40|
    41|His father's car keys lay on the counter. Ordinary keys—the kind any man carried in 1958—but they wore a puzzle fob that seemed to him a piece of art. A small wooden carving, Native American in design, interlocking geometric pieces fitted together with a precision that demanded investigation. Bob picked up the keys. The metal was cool against his palm. Bob turned the fob over and over, tracing the carved ridges where a craftsman's tool had met the wood.
    42|
    43|But childhood curiosity is a hungry animal. It cannot be satisfied long by one mystery when another waits nearby.
    44|
    45|As Bob twisted the fob in his small fingers, his eyes wandered the kitchen walls until they found what they sought: an electrical outlet. Twin slots, dark and silent, mounted in the wood paneling like a question mark without a curve.
    46|
    47|Bob knew the warnings. Every child in 1958 knew the warnings. "Don't put things in the outlet." His mother had said it. His father had said it. It was a rule as fixed as not running into the street. But rules are abstract things to a six-year-old. They're words without weight. The outlet was a mystery. The keys were in his hand. Those two facts began to circle each other like planets finding orbit, forming a question that demanded an answer.
    48|
    49|*What would happen?*
    50|
    51|---
    52|
    53|Bob remembered gripping the key shaft. Bob remembered his hand extending toward the outlet, a small astronaut reaching toward a new world. Bob remembered the twin slots waiting, dark and full of promise.
    54|
    55|The key made contact.
    56|
    57|Electricity is invisible. They see its fingerprints—light, heat, motion—but the current itself hides behind walls, a ghost they've domesticated. In that moment, Bob met that ghost directly. The shock surged through his body with the indifferent authority of physics acting on matter. His muscles clenched. His arm locked. The force threw him backward across the kitchen. Bob landed in a heap against the far wall.
    58|
    59|Darkness. Not the gentle dark of sleep, but a violent absence—a blink of the universe. His heart hammered against his ribs like a trapped thing. His hand—*oh, his hand*—tingled with a strange, persistent vibration, the echo of the current that had passed through it. Time became elastic. Those moments of disorientation stretched into what felt like hours. Bob sat on that linoleum floor, dazed, his body having learned something that all the warnings in the world could never teach.
    60|
    61|Then came the footsteps. Hurried. Panicked. His parents burst into the kitchen, their faces transformed—his mother's eyes wide, his father's jaw set. They found him crumpled against the wall, the keys on the floor between him and the outlet, the story written clearly without a single word spoken.
    62|
    63|The scolding came, as scoldings do. Words of admonishment dressed in fear, delivered in tones that betrayed how close they had come to something worse. Bob was told what Bob already knew, what his body had just learned in the most direct way possible: electricity was dangerous. The warnings, so abstract before, had found their weight.
    64|
    65|And yet.
    66|
    67|Here is the part that still surprises him, seventy years later. Despite the terror. Despite the scolding. Despite the tingle that lingered in his hand for hours afterward—Bob felt exhilaration. The shock had been a revelation. In touching that outlet, Bob had reached beyond the ordinary boundaries of childhood into a realm of invisible forces and physical laws. Bob had asked a question of the universe—*what will happen?*—and the universe had answered with unmistakable clarity. The pain was real. The fear was real. But so too was the learning, immediate and visceral, in a way no textbook or parental warning could ever achieve.
    68|
    69|This was science. This was discovery. This was the moment a child realizes the world operates according to principles that can be tested, that cause leads to effect with mathematical precision, that even the most dire warnings cannot compare to the power of direct experience.
    70|
    71|### What Bob Remember vs. What Bob Was Told
    72|
    73|But here they must pause, because Bob cannot be entirely certain this memory belongs to him. The mind is a trickster, a master forger of its own past. Cognitive science has proven this beyond doubt: every time they recall a memory, they reconstruct it. Details shift. Emotions intensify or fade. The boundary between what happened and what they believe happened becomes porous, eventually indistinguishable.
    74|
    75|His mother told the story of the electrical outlet many times as Bob grew up. She would recount it at family gatherings, shaking her head at her son's reckless curiosity. With each retelling, the story gained texture—his fascination with the puzzle fob, the exact sound of his body hitting the wall, the expression on his father's face. Did Bob remember these things? Or did Bob remembered *her* remembering them?
    76|
    77|The memory Bob carries feels real. Bob can feel the cool metal of the key. Bob can taste the ozone in the air afterward. But feeling real and *being* real are different things. A false memory can be as vivid, as certain, as one formed from actual experience. Bob has studied the neuroscience since then. Bob knows about synaptic plasticity, about long-term potentiation. But knowing the mechanism does not resolve the mystery. Bob still cannot say with certainty whether Bob remembered the shock itself or only remembers his mother telling him about it.
    78|
    79|Perhaps that ambiguity is itself the lesson.
    80|
    81|### The Spark That Lit a Life
    82|
    83|What is *not* ambiguous is the effect this event had on the course of his life. Whether Bob actually felt that jolt of electricity or merely believed Bob had, the result was the same: an awakening. The experience ignited something in him—a fascination with electricity that evolved into a passion for science and technology spanning seven decades.
    84|
    85|In the months and years that followed, Bob devoured books on electrical circuits with the hunger of someone who had tasted the power hidden in walls and wished to understand it. Bob conducted home experiments—some dangerous, all illuminating. Bob built gadgets from scrap parts, learning through trial and error the principles governing the invisible force that had once thrown him across a kitchen. His parents, recognizing that his curiosity could not be extinguished—only channeled—nurtured his endeavors. They bought him books. They tolerated the mess. They learned to check the fuse box after Bob had been "working" in the basement.
    86|
    87|That passion led to academic excellence in science, which led to university, which led to degrees in electrical and systems engineering. The little boy who touched the outlet grew into a man who would help design systems for NASA, who would contemplate missions to Mars, who would spend his professional life facing toward the stars.
    88|
    89|The gift of that moment was not merely vocational. It was philosophical. It taught him that understanding requires risk, that the pursuit of truth sometimes demands they touch the very things they're warned against. It taught him that the most formative moments of their lives might be partly—or entirely—fictional, and yet remain no less powerful for it. Whether Bob actually touched that outlet and felt that shock matters less than the fact that Bob *believe* Bob did—that this belief shaped his curiosity, his career, his very identity.
    90|
    91|The child still sits on that far kitchen floor, heart pounding, hand tingling, eyes wide with the terror and wonder of discovery. Whether it happened or not, it is true. It is the first chapter of a story about memory and identity, about how the past creates the present creates the future in an endless loop of becoming.
    92|
    93|That electrical spark—the literal shock and the metaphorical awakening it ignited—would have to wait for its perfect complement. Because something far more distant than a kitchen outlet was about to begin beeping its way across the night sky, and the child who had touched invisible forces in a Michigan cabin was about to discover that the universe held reaches extending far beyond anything he could yet imagine.
    94|
    95|Chapter Two: The Echoes of Sputnik and a Family Legacy
    96|
    97|The beep came from everywhere and nowhere at once in 1957. Five years old, Bob sat cross-legged on the worn linoleum floor of his grandparents' living room, eyes fixed on the radio console that dominated the corner like a mahogany cathedral. The voice on the broadcast spoke words Bob couldn't fully comprehend—something about Russians, a silver sphere now circling the Earth, a new age dawning while America slept. Beep. Beep. Beep. That sound—mechanical, relentless, somehow both cold and alive—lodged in his bones and stayed there for seven decades and counting.
    98|
    99|Bob didn't understand what Bob was witnessing. How could Bob? Bob was a child of the Midwest, raised in a world where televisions were still novelties and telephones came with party lines. The Space Age might as well have been the Stone Age for all the context his five-year-old mind could offer. But something about that beeping signal registered anyway, deep in his subconscious—a recognition that the world had shifted on its axis, that the comfortable boundaries of his young life had suddenly expanded to include not just his street and his town, but the infinite black canvas above.
   100|
   101|---
   102|
   103|If Sputnik represented humanity reaching upward, his family roots ran deep in the opposite direction—into iron rails and coal smoke and the rhythmic chug of locomotive engines. His grandfather was a locomotive engineer back when that title meant something almost sacred. In the early twentieth century, engineers weren't mere operators; they were craftsmen, masters of machines built by hand in foundries where every piston and valve bore the fingerprints of its maker. A photograph survives from that era: him perched atop an enormous black locomotive, his small hand gripping the cast-iron railing, his grandfather beside him with a wave that seemed to say, *This is yours, boy. This tradition of building, of making the immovable move—this is your inheritance.* Bob didn't remember the photograph being taken. Bob only remembers the photograph itself, studied so many times its edges softened and its colors faded into sepia.
   104|
   105|His great-grandfather, Robert Charters, carried the storytelling tradition further. When Bob was eight, the old man—already ravaged by consumption, eating baby food from glass jars that seemed to mock his diminished state—would summon him with a gesture learned in another century. "Remember, lad," he would rasp, his voice carrying the weight of Scottish highlands, Canadian wilderness, and the Michigan lumber camps where their family had finally put down roots. "We Mills have the blood of builders and engineers."
   106|
   107|Then came the stories that burned brightest. Knights Templar, he claimed—medieval warrior-monks who fought bloody Crusades, then transformed themselves into Europe's master builders, constructing the soaring Gothic cathedrals that still inspire awe. From protectors of pilgrims to moneylenders, from stone masons to bankers—the trajectory seemed improbable and somehow fitting for a family that would eventually produce locomotive engineers and, eventually, him.
   108|
   109|Years later, genealogical research found no documentary evidence of Templar connections. They were stories, embroidered and enhanced through generations of retelling until they achieved the density of myth. But sitting at that old man's bedside, watching his thin fingers gesture through the air as he described cathedrals rising from nothing, Bob didn't need proof. Whether his veins carried Templar blood was irrelevant. What mattered was that Bob believed himself part of a lineage of builders, of problem-solvers, of men who looked at raw materials and saw possibility. That belief shaped everything that followed. It still does.
   110|
   111|---
   112|
   113|To understand his father, you have to understand the crucible that forged him. Bob Sr. grew up an only child in a world bounded by an elementary school and a family home. When World War II erupted, it pulled him into something vast and terrifying. At seventeen, he enlisted in the Navy and found himself responsible for the electrical systems of a scow—a flat-bottomed workhorse that served the fleet in dangerous, unsung ways. He lived in cramped quarters with engine noise so constant it became a form of silence, snatched sleep in thirty-minute intervals between watches. He graduated to an aircraft carrier, where the stakes grew heavier. As a master electrician, he held lives in his hands every time he traced a circuit or repaired a generator. One mistake could mean planes unable to launch, pumps unable to fight fires, communications severed at the moment of maximum danger.
   114|
   115|He returned from the Pacific War changed, carrying things no seventeen-year-old should bear. He married his mother in a clandestine elopement—Catholic and Protestant, their families wouldn't bless the union, the old hatred running deep enough to cut. They moved into his parents' partially finished, unheated summer cottage, two young people trying to build a life in a structure meant for vacation weekends. Then came the recall.
   116|
   117|When North Korean forces poured across the 38th parallel in 1950, his father's decision to stay in the Naval Reserves—made for sensible peacetime reasons—became a doorway back into war. He served on an aircraft carrier through the Korean conflict, returning to Michigan only after the armistice of 1953. By then, his mother was pregnant with their first child, a boy they named Robert, after the generations of Roberts before him. The GI Bill bought what would otherwise have been impossible: a small home with a low-cost mortgage, a foothold in the American middle class for a working-class sailor with an elementary school education. Bob was born in the fall of 1952. A baby brother followed. The family was complete, or so it seemed.
   118|
   119|---
   120|
   121|His earliest coherent memories of his father are of a man in perpetual vigilance, as if still standing watch on a carrier deck. Saturdays in the Mills household were not days of rest. They were days of chores, inspections, tasks assigned with military precision and expected to military standards. He treated them not as children but as raw recruits who needed breaking down and rebuilding into capable men. For him, the firstborn, the emotional support he intended often got lost in translation, drowned out by the sheer volume of his voice. That voice. It wasn't that he was angry—not really—but he had learned to project authority across engine rooms and flight decks, to make himself heard over the scream of jets and the roar of machinery. When he brought that voice home, he thought he was preparing them for a world he knew to be unforgiving. What he never understood was that a child is not a sailor, and a living room is not a ship. Bob sees that now. Bob didn't then. Bob just knew that sound meant Bob had done something wrong, or was about to.
   122|
   123|His younger brother resisted passively. He would rock nervously, wait out the storm. But Bob took a different path. Bob learned to comply, to anticipate, to internalize the expectations until they became his own. Bob cleaned his room. Bob completed his chores without complaint. Bob tried, in essence, to become the model sailor his father wanted, never quite reaching the adult standards Bob would set for himself.
   124|
   125|There was tenderness in him, too, though it came sideways. He was a craftsman of extraordinary versatility—electrician by trade, but also plumber, carpenter, model builder. He found his peace in the garage, surrounded by the scent of sawdust and glue, constructing U-control and radio-controlled aircraft from balsa wood and tissue paper. These weren't toys; they were engineering challenges demanding the same precision as their full-sized counterparts. That garage became his summer classroom. He taught him to read blueprints, to calculate weight distributions, to understand the aerodynamic principles that kept fragile structures aloft. Other neighborhood boys joined them, drawn by the spectacle of flight and the quiet charisma of a man who could make the impossible seem achievable. He never turned a boy away. The garage became a sanctuary for a whole generation of young people seeking the approval of a father figure who demanded excellence and returned the satisfaction of creation. Years later, Bob recognized the pattern: his harshness and his generosity, his demanding nature and his dedication—all facets of a man trying to love his sons in the only language he knew. By the time his third brother arrived, his father had softened considerably. Experience taught him that children weren't sailors, that love didn't require drill sergeant volume. But for him, the firstborn, the die was already cast.
   126|
   127|---
   128|
   129|If the garage represented his father at his best, the dinner table was something more complicated. His parents carried the weight of their generation—the legacy of Depression-era scarcity and wartime rationing that had programmed their bodies to treat every meal as potentially the last. Providing food was love. Making children eat that food was responsibility. And ensuring nothing was wasted—*clean your plate*—was moral duty inherited from ancestors who knew genuine hunger.
   130|
   131|The problem was that his father had no conception of child-sized portions. He heaped their plates with adult quantities of meat and potatoes and vegetables. And when he said “clean your plate,” he meant it. They did not leave the table until every scrap was consumed.
   132|
   133|His younger brother rebelled. He would sit for hours, stubbornly refusing to finish, willing to endure punishment rather than force down food his body couldn’t accommodate. But Bob was different. Bob learned to eat. Bob cleaned his plate because that was what was expected, what was demanded, what made him worthy of his father’s approval. Bob ate past the point of fullness, past the point of comfort, past the point where his body sent clear signals of satiety. Slowly, inevitably, Bob lost track of what “full” even felt like.
   134|
   135|His parents never called him fat. They used the euphemism “husky,” as if the word itself could reshape reality. But the reality was that Bob grew up overweight—the product of forced consumption, of food tangled up with approval and safety and the avoidance of conflict. His father didn’t understand any of this. He was feeding his sons, ensuring they grew up strong, preparing them for a demanding world. That he might be programming his firstborn for a lifetime struggle with weight and health and self-image never occurred to him. He was overweight himself, locked in his own battles with the scale, unable to recognize the patterns he was passing down.

   139|### The Neuroscience of Addiction
   140|
   141|Neuroscience would later give Bob a language for what had happened to him. The brain’s reward circuits—the same pathways that evolved to reinforce survival behaviors like eating—had been hijacked by the very act of forced overconsumption. Each time Bob cleaned his plate past the point of fullness, his brain encoded a pattern: compliance equals safety equals reward. The dopamine system, designed to motivate seeking food in times of scarcity, learned instead to drive consumption in times of plenty.
   142|
   143|Bob’s father and mother were both overweight. They viewed providing food and making children eat it as part of their parenting role, a duty passed down from generations who had known genuine hunger. At dinner time Bob’s father would dish out an adult portion and require his son to eat it all. In his mind, making a child clean his plate was good parenting. His younger brother resisted, but Bob learned to eat it all, and in the process lost his sense of being full.
   144|
   145|The combination of bad habits, genetics, stress, and an impulsive personality helped Bob grow up overweight. His parents would never say he was fat—they would only describe Bob as “husky.” The word was a shield, a way of avoiding the truth that they had, through love and concern, set their son on a path toward a lifelong struggle.

   149|### The Adult Battle
   150|
   151|When Bob left home for college, freed from his father’s dinner table, he shed the pounds. The discipline he had learned in the garage—focus, persistence, attention to detail—served him well. He exercised, controlled his portions, found a weight that felt sustainable. For a few years, Bob was fit. Then came career, marriage, children, the inevitable stresses of supporting a family in a high-pressure world. Bob’s relationship with food morphed into a maze of emotions. It was no longer just about eating; it became a psychological crutch.
   152|
   153|The weight returned, and with it high blood pressure, diabetes, the slow accumulation of damage that excess weight inflicts. Unbeknownst to him, the food addiction that had started in childhood had deepened into something medical, something that neuroscientific research now links to the same memory circuits that record formative experiences. These circuits, once hijacked by addictive behaviors, become difficult to break free from.
   154|
   155|After his first wife died, the pattern accelerated. Bob’s life became a series of rendezvous with sugary, fatty, and salty temptations. He would often find himself in empty conference rooms at work, scavenging for stale donuts left over from morning meetings. The room would become a sanctuary, a place where he could momentarily escape the haunting void left by Nancy’s passing. The sugar and fat provided momentary relief from grief—a chemical holiday from the weight of loss.
   156|
   157|His body betrayed him, accumulating weight, bringing high blood pressure and diabetes deeper into his life. But it was not just the physical toll. Emotionally, he felt like a ship caught in a storm, tossed around by waves of anxiety and depression. The memory of his father’s voice—*Clean your plate or you will not leave the table*—echoed in his mind not as words but as something deeper, a pattern encoded in his nervous system, every time Bob reached for comfort.

   160|
   161|### The Road Back
   162|
   163|Yet the human spirit is resilient. Bob knew he was spiraling, and he also knew he had the power to pull himself back. The same determination that had carried him through engineering problems and career challenges now had to be turned inward. Through weight loss therapy and professional guidance, Bob discovered that his addiction was a complex web woven from genetic predispositions, environmental triggers, and deeply ingrained psychological patterns. He learned that memory plays a crucial role in eating disorders—it is not just about eating less, but about remembering the emotional states that food has been trained to alter.
   164|
   165|With newfound knowledge and professional help, Bob embarked on a years-long journey to reclaim his life, losing over two hundred pounds through exercise and strict weight management. The discipline that had served him in the garage and the boardroom now served him in the gym and at the dinner table. Years later, he gained back forty pounds, then lost them again. The fight is ongoing. Bob knows that food addiction, like any addiction, is something he will need to manage for the rest of his life.
   166|
   167|Understanding was the first step toward healing. Bob had traced a direct line from that childhood dinner table to his adult struggles, and in doing so had found the path back to himself. His father had been a good man who did not understand the impact of his parenting. Bob’s father himself was overweight and never intended harm. Studies show that early life experiences and memories significantly influence eating behaviors and disorders later in life. Bob had become living proof of that research—and also proof that the patterns can be broken.

Bob stands now at the intersection of all these memories, looking back with the clarity age provides and forward with the hope that has sustained him through every challenge. The echoes of 1957 still sound in his mind, but time and reflection have transformed them into something richer than recollection. They have become wisdom.

   180|Chapter Three: Mr. Chips
   181|
   182|The summer Bob turned seven, his father came home with a dog.
   183|
   184|Bob remembered the screen door slapping shut, that loose spring never quite catching. And then a sound Bob had never heard in their house before. Clicking. Nails on linoleum. And the softest, most tentative whimper from anything alive.
   185|
   186|His name was Mr. Chips, and he was a mongrel—a fierce protector for their family, his father announced. But he was wrong about that. Chips wasn't a guard dog. He was his first real friend.
   187|
   188|He had a coat as black as midnight, the kind that swallowed light, with a single white tip at the end of his tail—like someone had dipped it in paint as an afterthought. His eyes were brown, warm and uncertain, the eyes of an animal who had already learned the world could be cruel. His father bought him from a shelter, and you could see it in the way he moved those first few days. Careful. Measuring every step. Waiting for the other shoe to drop.
   189|
   190|The first time Bob touched him. Bob was sitting cross-legged on the kitchen floor, and he walked over slowly, head low, that white-tipped tail giving one tentative wag. He sniffed his hand—his nose cold and wet against his knuckles—and then he let out this sigh. Not a whimper. Just a long, slow exhale, like he'd been holding his breath his whole life and finally let it go. He laid his head on his knee, and Bob felt the weight of it. The warmth of his skull through his jeans. From that moment, they were inseparable.
   191|
   192|For four years, Chips and Bob were a unit. He slept at the foot of his bed every night, a warm, breathing lump that rose and fell in the dark. In the mornings his face would be inches from his, tail thumping against the mattress, waiting for him to wake up. His bark was sharp and sudden, a single explosive WOOF that startled him even when Bob knew it was coming. He smelled like dust and pine and something warm and animal Bob had never been able to name since.
   193|
   194|They played in the woods behind the house. Bob would throw sticks and he'd tear after them, crashing through ferns, that white-tipped tail disappearing into the green. He'd come back with leaves stuck to his fur and mud caked on his paws, tongue hanging out, looking at him like Bob was the best thing that had ever happened to him. And Bob thought maybe Bob was. He certainly was for him.
   195|
   196|Then one day he didn't come back.
   197|
   198|He'd run off into the woods, same as always. But the sun went down, and he wasn't at the door. His mother called and called into the dark. Nothing.
   199|
   200|They searched everywhere. His father, his mother, him—fanning out through the woods, calling his name until their voices went hoarse. His legs were scratched raw from branches. Bob remembered the silence between calls, that terrible waiting, listening for the jingle of his collar. It never came.
   201|
   202|Two days. Bob barely slept. Bob kept his spot at the foot of the bed open.
   203|
   204|On the third day, Bob found him.
   205|
   206|He was lying on the side of a country road, about a mile from the house. On his side, his black coat dull with dust, that white-tipped tail still against the gravel. The wind moved his fur, like he was just sleeping. But he wasn't sleeping. Bob knew from the way the world went quiet. From the way his legs stopped working.
   207|
   208|Bob knelt down. Bob touched his side. He was cold.
   209|
   210|Bob didn't cry right away. Bob just sat there on that gravel shoulder, his hand on his fur, staring at the trees across the road. Bob didn't know how long Bob stayed. Long enough for the shadows to shift. Long enough for a car to pass and not stop.
   211|
   212|This was his first experience with death, but it would not be his last. In the years to come, Bob would lose his grandparents. His first wife. Both of his parents. And Bob never felt like Bob understood any of it. Death is a part of life Bob has never fully understood. Bob was not sure anyone does.
   213|
   214|But Bob remembered that dog. Bob remembered the weight of his head on his knee. The sound of his bark. The way he looked at him like Bob was the only person worth following.
   215|
   216|And Bob remembered that stretch of gravel road, the wind moving through his fur, and the terrible stillness of a body that no longer held its soul.

   223|### 1961: A Friendship That Ended Too Soon
   224|
   225|In 1961, Bob was a young boy growing up in a world that was changing faster than anyone around him seemed to understand. The Space Race was accelerating. The Cold War pressed on. But for a nine-year-old, the biggest events happened at ground level, on the streets of his neighborhood and in the hallways of his school.
   226|
   227|His best friend was a Black American boy he met at school. Their friendship was the ordinary kind that children form without noticing—built on shared games, shared secrets, the wordless understanding that two people can have when they are young enough not to know why they should not be friends. They played after school, explored their neighborhood, and invented adventures that filled the long afternoons between the final bell and dinnertime.
   228|
   229|But one day, without explanation, the friendship ended. His friend’s parents, succumbing to the pressures of a society still deeply divided by race, forced their son to disassociate from Bob. There was no argument, no fight, no falling-out between the boys. Just an absence. A desk that remained empty. A space in the routines of childhood where a friend had been.
   230|
   231|This was Bob’s first encounter with the ugly face of discrimination. It would not be his last. As he grew older, the Civil Rights Movement began to gain momentum. Television screens filled with images of sit-ins, protests, and marches. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 was a landmark moment, but Bob understood even then that legislation alone could not change deeply ingrained attitudes. Discrimination and segregation persisted, not just against Black Americans but against other marginalized communities as well.
   232|
   233|Bob thought about this often. People discriminate against so many groups—Black, Jewish, Irish, Arab, Asian, Hispanic, fat people, gay people, trans people, women, immigrants, law enforcement, Native Americans, and others—he thought to himself. Why? Who is even left? This is crazy.
   234|
   235|Although a level of prejudice is ingrained in people who have been exposed to endemic discrimination all of their lives, Bob made a conscious decision early on: he would try to judge people by each person’s character, not by stereotyping. That lost friendship was a scar that taught him something no book ever could. The wound healed, but the lesson did not fade.
